questions.question: What is the optimal time complexity of Radix Sort when sorting N integers where each integer has d digits and each digit can take up to k distinct values?
questions.title: Radix Sort — optimal time complexity

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: **O(d × (N + k))** — d passes (one per digit), each pass doing a counting sort over N elements with k possible digit values.

questions.question: What is the worst-case time complexity of the Rabin-Karp string matching algorithm?
questions.title: Rabin-Karp — worst-case time complexity

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: **O(N × M)** (N = text length, M = pattern length) — occurs when hash collisions force character-by-character verification on every window (average case is O(N + M) with good hashing).

questions.question: Which design paradigm systematically builds a solution piece by piece, abandoning a path as soon as it determines the path cannot lead to a valid solution?
questions.title: Paradigm abandoning a path once it can't lead to a solution

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: **Backtracking** — it incrementally builds candidates and abandons ("prunes") a partial solution as soon as it's determined invalid, backtracking to try alternatives.

questions.question: Which of the following algorithmic paradigms is used in the Quick Sort algorithm?
questions.title: Algorithmic paradigm used in Quick Sort

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: **Divide and Conquer** — the array is partitioned around a pivot (divide), each partition sorted recursively (conquer), and no explicit merge step is needed since partitioning already places elements correctly relative to the pivot.

questions.question: When deleting a node with two children from a Binary Search Tree, what is the standard procedure to replace the deleted node's value?
questions.title: Deleting a BST node with two children
options: Delete it together with its whole subtree
Replace it with its inorder successor or predecessor, then delete that node
questions.answer: Replace it with its inorder successor or predecessor, then delete that node

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: Replace the node's value with its **inorder successor (the smallest value in its right subtree) or inorder predecessor (the largest value in its left subtree)**, then delete that successor/predecessor node (which has at most one child, making its removal simple).

questions.question: In the Knuth-Morris-Pratt (KMP) string matching algorithm, what does the precomputed longest proper prefix suffix (LPS) table primarily store for each position in the pattern?
questions.title: KMP — what the LPS table stores
options: The position of the last mismatch
The length of the longest proper prefix of the pattern that is also a suffix
The number of times each character occurs
questions.answer: The length of the longest proper prefix of the pattern that is also a suffix

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: For each position in the pattern, the LPS (Longest Proper Prefix which is also Suffix) table stores **the length of the longest proper prefix of the pattern (up to that position) that is also a proper suffix of it** — this lets the algorithm skip re-comparing characters after a mismatch.

questions.question: The 'Cut Property' is a fundamental concept used to prove the correctness of algorithms finding the:
questions.title: 'Cut Property' — proves correctness of which algorithms

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: The Cut Property underlies the correctness of **Minimum Spanning Tree algorithms (Prim's and Kruskal's)** — it states that for any cut (partition) of the graph's vertices, the minimum-weight edge crossing that cut must be part of some MST.

questions.question: Which data structure provides the most efficient way to track the median of a continuously expanding stream of integers?
questions.title: Data structure to track median of a data stream
options: Two heaps (a max-heap and a min-heap)
questions.answer: Two heaps (a max-heap and a min-heap)

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: **Two heaps** — a max-heap for the lower half of the numbers and a min-heap for the upper half, kept balanced in size — gives O(log N) insertion and O(1) median retrieval.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of evaluating a valid Postfix expression containing N tokens using a stack?
questions.title: Postfix expression evaluation using a stack — time complexity

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: **O(N)** — each of the N tokens is pushed/popped from the stack at most a constant number of times.

questions.question: What is the depth of the root node in a standard tree data structure?
questions.title: Depth of the root node in a tree

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: **0** (by standard convention, the root's depth is 0, since depth is measured as the number of edges from the root to that node).

questions.question: What is the optimal time complexity to perform both a point update and a range sum query on an array of size N using a binary indexed tree (Fenwick Tree)?
questions.title: Fenwick Tree (BIT) — point update & range sum query

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: **O(log N)** for both operations.

questions.question: What is the optimal time complexity to build a valid binary max-heap from an unsorted array of N elements using the bottom-up Heapify method?
questions.title: Building a binary max-heap from an unsorted array (bottom-up Heapify)

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: **O(N)** — although a single heapify call is O(log N) and there are N/2 non-leaf nodes, the total work sums to a geometric-like series that collapses to linear time, not O(N log N).

questions.question: Which algorithm is best suited for scheduling tasks with dependencies?
questions.title: Algorithm for scheduling tasks with dependencies

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: **Topological Sort** (on a Directed Acyclic Graph representing task dependencies) — it orders tasks so every dependency appears before the tasks that depend on it.

questions.question: In Tarjan's bridge-finding algorithm, an edge (u, v) in a Depth First Search (DFS) tree is classified as a critical bridge if and only if which condition is satisfied regarding the discovery time and low values?
questions.title: Tarjan's bridge-finding — condition for edge (u,v) to be a bridge

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: Edge (u, v), where v is a DFS-tree child of u, is a bridge if and only if **low[v] > disc[u]** — meaning v (and its subtree) cannot reach u or any of u's ancestors through any back edge, so removing (u, v) would disconnect the graph.

questions.question: What is the time complexity to search an element in a properly constructed Hash Table in the average case?
questions.title: Average-case search time in a hash table

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: **O(1)** — with a good hash function and load factor, lookups take constant time on average (worst case can degrade to O(N) with many collisions).

questions.question: Which variation of a linked list is best suited for implementing a continuous loop structure, such as a round-robin scheduler?
questions.title: Linked list variation best for a continuous loop (round-robin scheduler)

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: A **Circular Linked List** — the last node points back to the first, allowing continuous traversal without needing to detect a NULL end, ideal for round-robin cycling.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of finding the minimum element in an unsorted array of size N?
questions.title: Finding the minimum in an unsorted array of size N

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: **O(N)** — every element must be examined at least once since there's no ordering information to exploit.

questions.question: What is the primary characteristic of an articulation point in a connected graph?
questions.title: Primary characteristic of an articulation point
options: Removing it always leaves the graph connected
Removing it increases the number of connected components
It has the highest degree in the graph
questions.answer: Removing it increases the number of connected components

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: An articulation point (cut vertex) is a vertex whose **removal (along with its incident edges) increases the number of connected components in the graph** (disconnects the graph or a portion of it).

questions.question: What is the strict upper bound time complexity of the Edmonds-Karp algorithm for computing the maximum flow in a flow network with V vertices and E edges?
questions.title: Edmonds-Karp algorithm — upper bound complexity

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: **O(V × E²)** — it's the BFS-based (shortest augmenting path) implementation of Ford-Fulkerson, guaranteeing this polynomial bound regardless of edge capacities.

questions.question: Which data structure or paradigm does the Floyd-Warshall all-pairs shortest path algorithm utilize to systematically find shortest paths in a graph containing negative edge weights but no negative cycles?
questions.title: Floyd-Warshall — technique used

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: **Dynamic Programming** — it iteratively considers each vertex as a possible intermediate point in the shortest path between every pair of vertices, updating a distance matrix in O(V³) time, and correctly handles negative edge weights (as long as there's no negative cycle).

questions.question: Given an array of integers, which sorting algorithm is generally preferred if the array is already mostly sorted?
questions.title: Sorting algorithm preferred for a mostly-sorted array

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: **Insertion Sort** — it runs close to O(N) on nearly-sorted data since each element requires very few shifts to reach its correct position (adaptive algorithm).

questions.question: Which algorithmic strategy is used to solve the longest increasing subsequence problem in O(N^2) time?
questions.title: Solving Longest Increasing Subsequence in O(N²)
options: Greedy choice of the smallest element

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: **Dynamic Programming** — maintaining `dp[i]` = length of the longest increasing subsequence ending at index i, computed by checking all previous indices j < i.

questions.question: In a max-heap array representation, what is the index of the right child of a node at index 'i'? (Assuming 0-based indexing)
questions.title: Max-heap array — index of right child of node at index i (0-based)

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: **2i + 2** (left child is 2i + 1).

questions.question: Which graph algorithm effectively finds all Strongly Connected Components (SCCs) in a directed graph using a single Depth First Search (DFS) traversal combined with an explicit tracking stack?
questions.title: Finding all SCCs with a single DFS + explicit tracking stack

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: **Tarjan's Algorithm** — it uses discovery times, low-link values, and an explicit stack to identify strongly connected components in one DFS pass, unlike Kosaraju's algorithm which requires two DFS passes.

questions.question: In the Master Theorem for analyzing divide-and-conquer recurrences, what does the term 'a' represent in T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n)?
questions.title: Master Theorem — meaning of 'a' in T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n)
options: The depth of the recursion tree
The number of subproblems at each level of recursion
questions.answer: The number of subproblems at each level of recursion

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: **'a' represents the number of subproblems the recursive algorithm divides the original problem into at each level** (each of size n/b).

questions.question: What is the primary structural difference between a generic tree and a graph?
questions.title: Structural difference — generic tree vs graph
options: A tree is connected and acyclic; a general graph may contain cycles
A tree can have several paths between two nodes
A tree always has more edges than a graph
A graph must be directed; a tree is undirected
questions.answer: A tree is connected and acyclic; a general graph may contain cycles

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: A tree is a **connected, acyclic graph with exactly one path between any two nodes** (N nodes, N−1 edges, and a defined root/hierarchy) — a graph is a more general structure that **can contain cycles, multiple paths between nodes, and no required root/hierarchy**, and may even be disconnected.

questions.question: Which type of graph cannot contain a cycle by definition?
questions.title: Graph type that cannot contain a cycle by definition

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: A **Tree** (and more generally a **DAG — Directed Acyclic Graph** — for directed structures) cannot contain a cycle by definition.

questions.question: Which algorithm is used to compute the Longest Common Subsequence of two strings?
questions.title: Algorithm to compute Longest Common Subsequence

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: **Dynamic Programming** — building a 2D table `dp[i][j]` representing the LCS length of the first i characters of one string and first j characters of the other, in O(N×M) time.

questions.question: What is the amortized time complexity of a sequence of N push operations on an initially empty dynamic array that doubles its capacity whenever it becomes completely full?
questions.title: Amortized time for N pushes on a doubling dynamic array

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: **O(1) amortized per push** (O(N) total for N pushes) — although individual resize operations cost O(N), they happen so infrequently (doubling means resizes occur at 1, 2, 4, 8...) that the total cost across N pushes averages out to constant time per operation.

questions.question: What is the maximum possible height of an AVL tree containing N nodes, expressed as a strict asymptotic upper bound?
questions.title: Maximum height of an AVL tree with N nodes (asymptotic bound)

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: **O(log N)** — AVL trees maintain strict balance (height difference of subtrees ≤ 1 at every node), guaranteeing logarithmic height, unlike an unbalanced BST which can degrade to O(N).

questions.question: The 'Tower of Hanoi' problem is a classic example of which algorithmic approach?
questions.title: Tower of Hanoi — algorithmic approach

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: **Recursion** (and it's a classic example of the Divide and Conquer paradigm) — solving for N disks by first moving N−1 disks to an auxiliary peg, moving the largest disk, then moving the N−1 disks onto it.

questions.question: A Disjoint-Set (Union-Find) data structure is highly efficient for:
questions.title: Disjoint-Set (Union-Find) — highly efficient for
options: Tracking and merging groups of connected elements
Finding shortest paths in weighted graphs
questions.answer: Tracking and merging groups of connected elements

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: Efficiently **tracking and merging groups of connected elements and quickly answering "are these two elements in the same group/set?" queries** — classically used in Kruskal's MST algorithm and cycle detection in undirected graphs.

questions.question: What is the minimum number of spanning trees a connected unweighted graph with 'V' vertices and 'V-1' edges can have?
questions.title: Minimum spanning trees in a connected unweighted graph with V vertices, V−1 edges

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: **Exactly 1** — a connected graph with exactly V vertices and V−1 edges is by definition already a tree (no cycles, fully connected), so it IS its own unique spanning tree.

questions.question: Which data structure is internally used by Kahn's Algorithm to find a topological ordering of a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG)?
questions.title: Data structure internally used by Kahn's Algorithm for topological sort

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: A **Queue** (holding all vertices with in-degree 0 at each step) — vertices are dequeued, their outgoing edges "removed" by decrementing neighbors' in-degrees, and newly zero-in-degree vertices are enqueued.

questions.question: Which of the following data structures is most efficient for implementing an undo feature in a text editor?
questions.title: Best data structure for implementing an undo feature

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: A **Stack** — undo operations naturally follow LIFO order (the most recently performed action is the first one to be undone).

questions.question: In a weighted directed graph, which algorithm can detect the presence of a negative weight cycle?
questions.title: Algorithm detecting a negative weight cycle in a weighted directed graph

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: **Bellman-Ford Algorithm** — after running V−1 relaxation iterations, one additional relaxation pass; if any edge can still be relaxed further, a negative weight cycle exists.

questions.question: What is the minimum number of nodes in an AVL tree of height 2? (Assuming root is height 0)
questions.title: Minimum nodes in an AVL tree of height 2 (root = height 0)

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: 4 nodes.

questions.question: In a graph representing a computer network, which algorithm is best suited to find the minimum length of cable required to connect all computers?
questions.title: Algorithm for minimum cable to connect all computers in a network
options: A minimum spanning tree algorithm (Prim's or Kruskal's)
questions.answer: A minimum spanning tree algorithm (Prim's or Kruskal's)

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: A **Minimum Spanning Tree algorithm (Prim's or Kruskal's)** — it finds the subset of edges (connections) with minimum total weight (cable length) that connects all nodes without forming cycles.

questions.question: What is the optimal time complexity to compute the minimum number of scalar multiplications needed to multiply a chain of N matrices using classic dynamic programming?
questions.title: Optimal time complexity for Matrix Chain Multiplication (classic DP)

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: **O(N³)** — using a DP table over all possible chain split points, with O(N²) subproblems each taking O(N) to compute.

questions.question: The Breadth-First Search (BFS) algorithm uses which data structure to keep track of vertices to visit?
questions.title: Data structure used by BFS to track vertices to visit

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: A **Queue** (FIFO) — ensures vertices are explored level by level, in the order they were discovered.

questions.question: Given the Preorder and Inorder traversals of a binary tree, what is the best time complexity to uniquely reconstruct the entire original binary tree architecture?
questions.title: Reconstructing a binary tree from Preorder + Inorder — best time complexity

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: **O(N)** — achievable using a hash map to store inorder indices for O(1) root-position lookups, avoiding the naive O(N²) linear search approach.

questions.question: What is the fundamental approach behind the 'Divide and Conquer' algorithm strategy?
questions.title: Fundamental approach behind 'Divide and Conquer'
options: Always pick the locally best choice
Try all possibilities and undo bad choices
Split into smaller subproblems, solve them recursively, then combine the results
Store results of overlapping subproblems in a table
questions.answer: Split into smaller subproblems, solve them recursively, then combine the results

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: **Break the problem into smaller independent subproblems of the same type (divide), solve each subproblem recursively (conquer), and then combine their solutions to solve the original problem (combine).**

questions.question: What data structure would be most appropriate for implementing a printer queue?
questions.title: Data structure appropriate for a printer queue

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: A **Queue** — print jobs are processed in the order they were submitted (FIFO), matching a queue's natural behavior.

questions.question: Which state representation technique is typically used in dynamic programming to efficiently solve the traveling salesman problem for a small graph with N vertices?
questions.title: DP state representation for small-N Traveling Salesman Problem

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: **Bitmask Dynamic Programming** — the state is represented as `dp[mask][i]`, where `mask` is a bitmask indicating the set of visited cities and `i` is the current city, enabling an O(N² × 2ᴺ) solution (Held-Karp algorithm).

questions.question: The process of removing the root element and restructuring the remaining elements to maintain the heap property is called:
questions.title: Removing root and restructuring to maintain heap property

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: This operation is called **Heapify (specifically, "sift-down" or "heapify-down")** — after removing the root, the last element is moved to the root position and repeatedly swapped downward with its larger/smaller child until the heap property is restored (this whole extraction process is often just called "extract-min/max").

questions.question: When implementing a Disjoint Set Union (DSU) data structure with both path compression and union by rank optimizations, what is the amortized time complexity per operation?
questions.title: DSU with path compression + union by rank — amortized time per operation

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: **O(α(N))**, where α is the inverse Ackermann function — this grows so slowly that it's effectively constant (near O(1)) for all practical input sizes.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of binary search on a sorted array of N elements?
questions.title: What is the time complexity of binary search on a sorted arr

sections.label: Theory
sections.content: Binary search repeatedly halves the search space by comparing the target to the middle element.

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: **O(log N)** — each comparison eliminates half of the remaining elements, so the search space shrinks exponentially, requiring only about log₂N comparisons in the worst case.

questions.question: What is the main advantage of a hash table over a balanced BST for lookups?
questions.title: What is the main advantage of a hash table over a balanced B
options: Average-case O(1) lookup versus O(log N) for a BST
Hash tables always use less memory
Hash tables keep elements sorted automatically
questions.answer: Average-case O(1) lookup versus O(log N) for a BST

sections.label: Theory
sections.content: Both support fast lookups, insertions, and deletions, but with different complexity guarantees and trade-offs.

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: **A well-implemented hash table offers average-case O(1) time for lookup, insert, and delete, versus O(log N) for a balanced BST** — the trade-off is that hash tables don't maintain sorted order and can degrade to O(N) with poor hashing/many collisions, while BSTs maintain sorted order and guarantee O(log N) even in the worst case (if balanced).

questions.question: Why is Dijkstra's algorithm unsuitable for graphs with negative edge weights?
questions.title: Why is Dijkstra's algorithm unsuitable for graphs with negat
options: It greedily finalizes the shortest distance to a node, which can be invalidated by a later negative edge
It cannot handle graphs with more than 100 nodes
It only works on trees, not general graphs
Negative weights cause an infinite loop in the priority queue
questions.answer: It greedily finalizes the shortest distance to a node, which can be invalidated by a later negative edge

sections.label: Theory
sections.content: Dijkstra's is a greedy algorithm that assumes once a node's shortest distance is finalized, it can never be improved.

sections.label: Answer
sections.content: **Dijkstra's greedily 'locks in' the shortest known distance to each node as soon as it's popped from the priority queue, assuming it can never be improved later — but a negative-weight edge encountered afterward could actually produce a shorter path, violating that assumption** and giving incorrect results. (Bellman-Ford handles negative weights correctly, at the cost of higher time complexity.)
